citation: Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu, Olivia T. Karaman, Jason Hawes, Gabriella Rosen Kellerman. 'When Using AI Leads to "Brain Fry"'. Harvard Business Review, Generative AI section, 5 March 2026. https://hbr.org/2026/03/when-using-ai-leads-to-brain-fry ; BCG summary page https://www.bcg.com/news/5march2026-when-using-ai-leads-brain-fry
source_tier: Consultancy research published as a practitioner article in a business magazine (not peer-reviewed; no methods appendix seen)

Re-opened 21 Oct 2026: HBR live page returned only the title, byline and truncated summary (no body). BCG page returned only a short summary ('Based on a BCG study of 1,488 US workers across large companies') with none of the percentages. No BCG Henderson Institute detail page was found or opened. All figures and quotes below come from the printed copy.
sponsor_and_incentive: Authors are BCG staff: Bedard (Managing Director & Partner, BCG Henderson Institute Fellow), Kropp (Senior Partner, CTO of BCG X, BHI Fellow), Hsu (Project Leader, BHI Ambassador), Kellerman (Expert Partner and Director). Karaman and Hawes are UC Riverside PhD candidates who are also BCG research assistants. The article states no funder. BCG sells AI strategy and people-transformation advice, and the article recommends that 'A full 70% of AI transformation efforts should be devoted to people and processes', which is close to BCG's service line.
exact_quotes: 'AI brain fry, which we define as mental fatigue from excessive use or oversight of AI tools beyond one's cognitive capacity.' (para after sample description)

'we conducted a study of 1,488 full-time U.S.-based workers (48% male vs 51% female; 58% independent contributors vs 41% leaders) at large companies across industries, roles, and levels. We asked them about patterns and quantity of AI use, work experiences, and cognition and emotions.' (opening of methods paragraph)

'The workers in our study who reported that their AI work required high rather than low degrees of oversight expended 14% more mental effort on the job. A high degree of AI oversight also predicted 12% more mental fatigue for participants. Finally, more intensive AI oversight also predicted 19% greater information overload' (section 'When AI Use Predicts Mental Fatigue')

'As employees go from using one AI tool to two simultaneously, they experience a significant increase in productivity. As they incorporate a third tool, productivity again increases, but at a lower rate. After three tools, though, productivity scores dipped.' (same section; preceded by 'perceived productivity increases')

'Fourteen percent of participants in our study using AI for work endorsed the experience of AI brain fry.' (section 'Introducing AI Brain Fry'; asked at the end of the survey 'to avoid priming effects')
'Workers in our study who endorsed AI brain fry experience 33% more decision fatigue than those who did not.' (section 'The Business Cost')

'Among participants using AI at work, those experiencing brain fry reported making mistakes significantly more often— scoring 11% and 39% higher on the minor and major error frequency measures, respectively—than those who did not.'

'We defined minor errors as "small errors that are easy to catch or correct, such as coding or formatting errors" and major errors as "errors with more serious consequences, such as those that could affect safety, outcomes, or important decisions."'

'Among workers who did not report AI brain fry, 25% showed active intent to leave. Among those who did report AI brain fry, that rose to 34%. This represents a 39% increase in active worker intent to leave among top users of AI.'
'Quantitatively, we found strong correlations between AI brain fry and information overload, but a less straightforward relationship with items related to task switching.'
'Our research suggests adverse productivity gains after the use of three AI agents at the same time.' (Lessons for Leaders)

'AI oversight cannot simply be layered on top of human oversight; nor can AI agents be stacked on one user ad infinitum. Just as we have norms for spans of control for managing humans, so, too, limits need to be defined for human + agent oversight and for agents alone.'

'Acute mental fatigue, on the other hand, is caused by marshalling attention, working memory, and executive control beyond the limited capacity of these systems. This is exactly what intensive AI oversight requires.'
'our study suggests that use of AI tools may be causing the mental exhaustion itself.' (hedged causal language)
'Just because a worker can keep iterating with AI at a low marginal cost does not mean they should.'
Engineer quote: 'I end each day exhausted—not from the work itself, but from the managing of the work.' (Francesco Bonacci, X post, cited as motivating anecdote)
date_and_recency: Published 5 March 2026. Data collection window not stated in the printed copy [uncertain]. Article says online posts appeared 'in recent weeks', so the survey likely ran in early 2026 [uncertain].
key_claims: Intensive oversight of AI tools produces acute mental fatigue ('AI brain fry'), distinct from burnout. Oversight was the most mentally taxing form of AI engagement. Brain fry is linked to decision fatigue, self-reported errors and intent to quit. Using AI to replace repetitive tasks is linked to lower burnout (but not lower mental fatigue). Manager, team and organisational practices (answering questions, organised integration, clear strategy, work-life balance signals) are linked to lower fatigue. Leaders should set limits on human-plus-agent oversight, shift metrics from activity to impact, and track cognitive load.
headline_figures: n = 1,488 full-time US workers at large companies; 48% male, 51% female; 58% independent contributors, 41% leaders.
High vs low AI oversight: 14% more mental effort; 12% more mental fatigue; 19% greater information overload (all 'predicted', i.e. associations).
14% of participants using AI for work endorsed having experienced AI brain fry (single yes/no style item asked at the end of the survey).

Prevalence by function: 6% legal (low) to 26% marketing (high); after marketing: people operations, operations, engineering, finance, IT highest. Engineering's own percentage is not given in the text (chart only) [uncertain].
Brain fry vs no brain fry: 33% more decision fatigue; error frequency measures 11% higher (minor) and 39% higher (major); active intent to leave 25% vs 34%.

Intent to quit arithmetic: 25% to 34% is a 9 percentage point rise, a relative rise of 36% (9/25). The article calls it '39% increase'. 39% is not reproduced by these rounded figures (possible unrounded values or a different calculation, not explained).
Using AI to cut routine tasks: burnout scores 15% lower than non-users of AI in that way.

Manager answers AI questions: 15% lower mental fatigue; manager expects staff to work it out alone: 5% higher ('AI orphan tax'); org expects more work due to AI: 12% higher mental fatigue; org values work-life balance: 28% lower mental fatigue.

Tools simultaneously: productivity rises from 1 to 2 tools, rises more slowly with a third, dips after three. Measure is perceived/self-reported productivity across all AI tool types (search, research, data analysis, image, coding agents), no numbers given in text.

Unit for percentages is difference in mean scale scores between groups (relative %), not percentage of people, except 14%, 6%, 26%, 25%, 34% which are shares of people. Scales and instruments are not described in the text [uncertain].
sample_unit_and_population: 1,488 full-time US-based workers at large companies across industries, roles and levels; 58% individual contributors, 41% leaders. Not a software-engineer sample: tools spanned search agents, research agents, data analysis, image/design tools and coding agents. Engineering was one of several functions with higher brain-fry prevalence. Recruitment method and panel not stated in the printed copy [uncertain]. Software developers are mentioned only in a separate remark: 'In our work with software developers, we've found that the ones who are most advanced with AI start to feel blocked...' (not part of the survey data).
observed_vs_stated: Entirely self-reported survey: AI use patterns, oversight level, mental effort, fatigue, information overload, decision fatigue, errors (self-reported frequency), intent to quit and perceived productivity. No observed behaviour, physiology, error audits or retention data. Brain fry itself is a self-endorsed single item, supplemented by open-text descriptions ('fog', 'buzzing', headaches).
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Authors say acute fatigue comes from 'marshalling attention, working memory, and executive control beyond the limited capacity of these systems'. Oversight plus increased workload widens 'sphere of accountability', 'requiring them to pay attention to more outcomes for more tools in the same amount of time'. Qualitative accounts point to information overload and task switching; the data link strongly to information overload but only 'less straightforward' to task-switching items. The engineering manager quote: 'double-checking every little thing', 'working harder to manage the tools than to actually solve the problem'.
consequence_for_quality: Self-reported: more decision fatigue (33%), more minor and major errors (11%, 39% higher frequency scores), higher intent to quit (25% vs 34%). The authors also infer, without measuring it, that cultures prioritising cognitive thriving 'can expect to see better judgments, fewer errors, and higher retention'. Their $150M-per-year suboptimal-decision cost for a $5B firm is from a 2018 study they cite, applied loosely ('could increase that cost by millions').
what_reduces_the_load: Limits on simultaneous agents per person (spans of control for human-plus-agent oversight; adverse perceived productivity after three); embed AI in team workflows as a collective capability; manager who answers AI questions (15% lower fatigue); clear AI strategy and training (directional only); avoid team pressure to use AI and large variation in use; clear workload expectations; work-life balance signals (28% lower); metrics based on impact not token or usage volume; do not immediately backfill automated work; upskill in problem framing, analysis planning and prioritisation; track cognitive load in people analytics; design tools needing less intense attention or working memory. Replacing routine tasks lowers burnout but, per the article, not mental fatigue scores.
limitations_stated: The printed copy states no formal limitations section. The authors use hedged language in places: 'predicted', 'directionally', 'seemed to', 'our study suggests that use of AI tools may be causing the mental exhaustion itself'. They concede the task-switching link is 'less straightforward' and that the organisational practices only 'seemed to help'. No mention of cross-sectional design, common-method bias, self-selection, or effect sizes / significance tests for most figures.
counter_evidence: Own findings: AI used to replace routine work is linked to lower burnout; the literature has 'mixed signals' (some studies show AI reduces exhaustion). Methodological critique (mine, not from the article): cross-sectional self-report with single-item brain fry measure, so causality cannot be inferred and people already fatigued or intending to quit may both rate AI oversight as heavy and report errors; consultancy authors with a commercial interest; productivity-after-three-tools is perceived productivity across all tool types, not coding agents or measured output. I did not open any independent critique or replication [uncertain].
verification_status: All figures and quotes checked against the printed copy of the HBR article (opened and read in full). The BCG page was re-opened and confirms only the 1,488 sample and the headline claim (errors, decision overload, intent to quit); it carries no percentages. Live HBR page not readable (paywalled). No BCG Henderson Institute detail page found, so methods, scales and data window are NOT verified against a primary methods source [uncertain]. The arithmetic check (36% vs 39%) is mine. Press misreports of the 33% and 11%/39% figures were not checked here, so none is relied on.
usable_claim: In a BCG survey of 1,488 US workers at large companies (self-reported), people who said their AI work needed high oversight reported 14% more mental effort and 12% more mental fatigue than those with low oversight. Fourteen percent of AI users said they had experienced 'AI brain fry', and those people reported more decision fatigue, more errors and higher intent to quit. The authors call for limits on how many agents one person oversees. Say 'reported' and 'associated with', and note the authors are BCG consultants.
do_not_use: Do not say brain fry causes errors, quitting or lost productivity. Do not use '39% increase' in intent to quit (25% to 34% is 9 points, or 36% relative); say 'from 25% to 34%'. Do not describe 33% as the share of workers or as a rate of errors: it is higher decision-fatigue score. Do not say the 11% and 39% are shares of people making errors; they are higher error-frequency scores. Do not say productivity falls after three coding agents: it is perceived productivity across mixed AI tools. Do not use $150M figure as this study's finding. Do not use press paraphrases of the study. Do not say software engineers specifically were studied.
